hooks: From Hadrianopolis, founded by the emperor Hadrian — worn down through Greek to Edirne.
It was the Ottoman capital for almost a century before Constantinople fell, and the Selimiye mosque here is Sinan's masterpiece and a UNESCO site.
Its oil wrestling tournament at Kırkpınar has been held every year since 1346, the oldest continuously running sporting event in the world.
A recent name, probably from a local word for a marshy meadow — one of the few provinces without an ancient name.
Turkey's only hard coal basin, worked since 1848, and its mines run out under the Black Sea.
The coal here fuelled the Ottoman navy and then the republic's first industry.
From Greek Amisos, with the Turkish prefix worn on from "eis Amison", "to Amisos".
Atatürk landed here on 19 May 1919 to begin the war of independence, which is why that date is a national holiday.
It sits on the delta of the Kızılırmak, Turkey's longest river, and grows most of the country's tobacco.
"Black bend" or "black bush" — kara, black, plus a word for a river bend.
Created around the steelworks built here in 1937, the republic's first heavy industry project.
Safranbolu in it has hundreds of preserved Ottoman merchant houses and is a UNESCO site.
From Greek Rhizaion, from rhiza, a root or a foothill.
It grows nearly all of Turkey's tea, planted from the 1920s after the loss of coffee-growing lands made an alternative urgent.
The wettest province in the country, over 2,200 mm a year, and its Ayder plateau is Alpine meadow above the cloud.
From Greek eis tin polin, "to the city" — travellers said where they were going and the phrase became the name.
The only city on two continents, and it was the capital of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires in turn for 1,600 years.
Hagia Sophia's dome, finished in 537, was the largest in the world for nearly a thousand years.
Turkish for "army" — the name of a camp that became a town; the same word gives English "horde".
It produces a large share of Turkey's hazelnuts, and Turkey grows about 70% of the world's.
Boztepe above the town is reached by cable car and looks down the whole coast.
"Tekfur mountain" — tekfur was the Turkish word for a Byzantine lord, so the name means the lord's mountain.
Its rakı is the most respected in Turkey, distilled from Thracian grapes and aniseed.
The Ganos ridge along its coast was known in antiquity for wine and is still terraced for it.
From Greek Trapezous, "table" — the flat-topped hill the city was built on.
It was the capital of a Greek empire of its own, Trebizond, which outlasted Constantinople by eight years until 1461.
The Sumela monastery near it clings to a cliff face 300 m up, founded in 386.
From Nicomedia, through Greek "eis Nikomedian" — the same worn-down construction as Istanbul and Izmir.
It was the eastern capital of the Roman Empire under Diocletian, before Constantinople was built.
The 1999 earthquake here killed over 17,000 people and reshaped Turkish building regulation.
"Island market" — ada island, pazar market: a market on land ringed by river branches.
It is the capital of Sakarya province and the centre of Turkey’s railway rolling-stock industry.
The 1999 earthquake struck here too, and parts of the town sank into liquefied ground.
Of uncertain origin — possibly from Çorumlu, a tribal name, or from a word meaning a mixed place.
Hattusa here was the Hittite capital, and its archive of clay tablets gave the world its first known peace treaty, with Egypt.
It produces most of Turkey's leblebi, roasted chickpeas, and its clay is used for bricks nationwide.
Possibly from a word for a fortified place, or from Armenian or Greek origins that are now unclear.
Its printed cloth, yazma, is block-printed by hand using techniques unchanged for centuries.
The Roman bridge at Tokat and the Hittite site at Maşat Höyük both show how long this pass has been used.
From Prusa, named for Prusias, the king of Bithynia who founded it around 200 BC.
The first Ottoman capital, and its early mosques and tombs are a UNESCO site.
Turkish silk was woven here, the İskender kebab was invented here, and Uludağ above it is the country's best-known ski mountain.
From Ancyra, Greek for "anchor" — the Galatians or the Phrygians are said to have found one here, far from any sea.
Atatürk made it the capital in 1923 over Istanbul, deliberately choosing a small Anatolian town of 30,000 people.
The Angora goat, cat and rabbit are all named after it, and its mohair was a protected Ottoman export.
From Arz-ı Rum, "the land of the Romans" — Rum meaning Byzantine, which is what the Turks called them.
The highest large city in Turkey at 1,900 m, and one of the coldest; it hosted the 2011 Winter Universiade.
Its Çifte Minareli Medrese from the 1200s is one of the finest Seljuk buildings anywhere.
"Forty castles" — kırk forty, kale castle, though the name may really be from a village called Kırıkköy.
Founded around a state arms factory in 1925 and made a province in 1989, so it is one of the newest.
It has the country's largest oil refinery inland, at the junction of the main east–west pipelines.
"Old city" — the Turkish name for what had been Dorylaeum, a Byzantine town.
Meerschaum, the white stone smoking pipes are carved from, is mined almost nowhere else in the world.
It is Turkey's most student-heavy city and has a reputation as its most liveable.
From Erez, an old Armenian settlement name, with a Persian diminutive.
Destroyed by earthquakes repeatedly, most catastrophically in 1939 when about 33,000 people died — the deadliest in Turkish history.
The Kemaliye gorge road here was cut through cliffs by hand by villagers over 132 years.
From Sebasteia, named for Augustus — sebastos is the Greek translation of the Latin augustus.
The 1919 congress held here set the terms of the independence movement, and the building is now a museum.
Its Divriği hospital and mosque, with carved portals unlike anything else in Islamic architecture, is a UNESCO site.
From Palaiokastron, Greek for "old castle", worn down through Turkish.
It has coast on both the Aegean and the Marmara, the only province on both.
Kaz Dağı in it is the ancient Mount Ida, where the judgement of Paris is set and from which the gods watched the Trojan War.
From Cotyaeum, a Phrygian and then Roman town.
Its tiles and ceramics have been made since the 1400s and decorated mosques across the empire after Iznik's kilns declined.
Aizanoi in the province has the best-preserved temple of Zeus in Anatolia and the world's first known stock exchange building.
"Opium black castle" — afyon is opium, kara black, hisar fortress: the poppy fields and the black rock the citadel sits on.
Turkey is one of the few countries licensed to grow opium poppies for the world's legal medical morphine, and most of it is grown here.
Its thermal springs are the most used in Turkey, and its clotted cream and Turkish delight are national brands.
From Caesarea, named for Caesar — Tiberius renamed the Cappadocian capital Mazaca after Augustus.
Mount Erciyes above it is an extinct volcano of 3,864 m whose ash created the Cappadocian landscape next door.
Its merchants are proverbial in Turkey for shrewdness, and the city has more industrial exporters than almost any other.
Turkish for "servant" or "young man", though the name may predate that reading.
Its carpets were exported to Europe from the 1500s and appear in Holbein's and Lotto's paintings — which is why dealers call the patterns Holbein and Lotto carpets.
The Karun treasure, Lydian gold looted from here, was recovered from New York in 1993 after a long legal fight.
From El-Aziz, "the glorious", named for Sultan Abdülaziz in 1866 and later Turkified.
Harput above it is the old town, abandoned for the new one on the plain.
Its Keban dam created a lake that drowned the old town of Ağın and several archaeological sites.
From Magnesia ad Sipylum — and the same Magnesia gives us magnet, magnesium and manganese.
The Ottoman princes trained here as well as at Amasya, and its Mesir festival has distributed a spiced paste as medicine since 1527.
Mount Sipylus above it has a natural rock face the Greeks took for Niobe weeping, which Homer mentions.
From Biainili, the Urartians' own name for their kingdom — the name is nearly three thousand years old.
Lake Van is Turkey's largest and is soda water, seven times saltier than the sea, with only one fish species able to live in it.
The Van cat has one blue eye and one amber, and swims — unusual in a cat.
From Smyrna, through Greek "eis Smyrnen" — the same "to the city" construction that produced Istanbul.
One of the candidates for Homer's birthplace, and continuously inhabited for about 8,500 years.
Ephesus in the province had the Temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders, and its library facade is the image of Roman Asia.
From Hittite Melid or Maldiya, meaning honey — a name over three thousand years old.
It grows about 80% of the world's dried apricots.
Aslantepe mound in it is a UNESCO site with one of the oldest known palaces and the earliest swords ever found.
From Aramaic or Arabic, possibly Se'ert, "city", or from an older Assyrian name.
Its pistachios are a distinct variety, and the province gives its name to the Siirt blanket, woven from mohair.
The Botan valley here is one of the deepest canyons in Turkey.
"The land of the Bakr" — diyar is land or abode, Bakr the Arab tribe that settled here in the 600s.
Its black basalt walls run 5.8 km, second in length only to the Great Wall by an old claim, and are a UNESCO site.
It is the largest Kurdish-majority city in Turkey, and its watermelons were once grown so large they were carried by camel.
Nothing to do with the comic: it is from the Batman river, and batman was also an Ottoman unit of weight.
The city grew from a village of 3,000 to a city on oil found here in 1940.
Hasankeyf in the province, a 12,000-year-old town, was flooded by the Ilısu dam in 2020 after a long international campaign to save it.
From Iconium, which the Greeks explained with a story about an eikon, an image, set up here.
Rumi lived, wrote and died here, and the whirling dervish ceremony his followers developed is a UNESCO heritage item.
The largest province in Turkey by area, and its plain grows most of the country's grain — it is called Turkey's breadbasket.
Named for the Aydınoğulları, a Turkish beylik that ruled the region after the Seljuks; aydın also means bright.
It grows more figs than anywhere in the world, and the Aegean fig is Turkey's oldest protected export.
Aphrodisias in it was a city of marble sculptors whose work reached across the Roman empire; it is a UNESCO site.
"With sea" — which is odd for an inland province; the name probably referred to abundant water rather than the sea.
Pamukkale here is a hillside of white travertine terraces filled with warm water, a UNESCO site.
Hierapolis on top of it was a Roman spa town, and its Plutonium emitted enough carbon dioxide to kill sacrificial animals, which the priests presented as a miracle.
"The unfortunate man" in Turkish by folk etymology; the older name was Hısn-ı Mansur, the fortress of Mansur.
Mount Nemrut here has the colossal heads of a first-century BC king's tomb sanctuary, and is a UNESCO site.
That king, Antiochus I of Commagene, had himself carved among Greek and Persian gods as their equal.
From Greek Sparta or from Baris — the derivation is contested; it has nothing to do with the Peloponnesian Sparta beyond the name.
It produces a large share of the world's rose oil, distilled from Rosa damascena picked before dawn in May.
It takes about 4,000 kg of petals to make one kilogram of oil, which is why the oil is priced like a precious metal.
"Heroic Maraş" — the title was added in 1973 for the town's resistance to French occupation in 1920.
Its ice cream is made with salep and mastic, stretchy enough to be cut with a knife and eaten with a fork.
The February 2023 earthquake had its epicentre in this province and killed over 50,000 people across the region.
Named for the Karamanid beylik, the Seljuks' strongest successor, which held out against the Ottomans until 1487.
In 1277 the Karamanid ruler decreed that only Turkish would be used in government — the first such order, and marked in Turkey as Language Day.
Its Binbirkilise, "a thousand and one churches", is a field of ruined Byzantine chapels on a volcanic slope.
"Glorious Urfa" — the title was added in 1984 for its resistance in 1920; Urfa is from Edessa, through Syriac Urhai.
Göbekli Tepe here is the oldest known monumental architecture in the world, about 11,500 years old — older than farming, pottery or writing.
Abraham is said by local tradition to have been born in a cave in the city, which makes it a pilgrimage site for three religions.
"Veteran Antep" — gazi was added in 1921 for the town's siege resistance; Antep is probably from Aïntab, "good spring".
It is Turkey's gastronomic capital and a UNESCO City of Gastronomy; its baklava has protected status.
The Zeugma mosaic museum here holds mosaics rescued from a Roman city flooded by a dam, including the Gypsy Girl.
From ancient Nisibis, a Mesopotamian city on the Roman-Persian frontier.
Its School of Nisibis was a major centre of Syriac learning from the fourth century, sometimes called an early university.
The Syrian border runs along the edge of the town, dividing it from Qamishli on the other side.
Possibly from Adanos, a figure in Hittite myth, or from a word related to the Danuna people.
Its kebab is a national institution, and the province is the centre of Turkish cotton.
The Taşköprü bridge over the Seyhan was built in the Roman period and carried traffic until 2007.
An ancient name of unclear origin, recorded by the Hittites as Tarsa.
St Paul was born here, and Cleopatra sailed up its river to meet Mark Antony in 41 BC.
The Cilician Gates above it are the pass through the Taurus that every army crossing Anatolia has used.
From Attaleia, founded by Attalus II of Pergamon in about 150 BC and named for himself.
It is one of the most visited cities in the world by international arrivals, and its Konyaaltı and Lara beaches run for kilometres.
The Lycian Way along its coast is a 540 km waymarked path past rock tombs cut into cliffs.
Possibly from the myrtle, mersin in Turkish, which grows along this coast.
Turkey's largest container port, and the terminus of the road to Syria and the Gulf.
Its Kızkalesi is a castle on an island 200 m offshore, with a matching one on the beach.
"Little Alexander" — Alexandretta, founded by Alexander the Great after his victory at Issus nearby in 333 BC.
It was the Mediterranean outlet for Aleppo for centuries, and its hinterland is Arabic-speaking.
Turkey’s main naval base on the eastern Mediterranean is here.
From Antioch, founded around 300 BC by Seleucus and named for his father Antiochus.
It was the third city of the Roman Empire, and the followers of Jesus were first called Christians here.
Its mosaic museum holds one of the largest collections in the world; the 2023 earthquake destroyed much of the old town.
